item.title: Seasonal surface melt onset and firn freeze-up across the central Wrangell and St. Elias Mountains
item.dc:creator: Ingalise Kindstedt, Andrew Johnson, Kristin M. Schild, Luke Copland, Christine Dow, Alison Criscitiello, … (+3)
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: surface melt, firn
Mountain snow at high elevations is changing as warming causes more melting and water to linger within it. We use satellite radar images from 2015 to 2024 to track when melting starts and when snow refreezes across the Wrangell and St. Elias Mountains on the border of Alaska and Yukon. We find that melting now reaches nearly all elevations, and water often remains trapped well into fall. Only the highest areas stay fully dry, showing widespread impacts of warming on mountain snowpacks.

item.title: A standardized permafrost ground temperature collection for Canada 2025
item.dc:creator: Olivia Meier-Legault, Nicholas Brown, Larry Adjun, Michel Allard, Alejandro Alvarez, Maude Auclair, … (+45)
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: permafrost
Ground temperature data is vital for permafrost and climate research yet data is often fragmented. We created a standardized collection of ground temperatures from over 900 sites across Canada. From 42 published and unpublished sources, we manually verified, cleaned and standardized data with a new software tool. This dataset supports permafrost research on a nationwide scale and can help improve models by acting as a reliable benchmark.

item.title: Generative modelling for multivariate spatio-temporal downscaling of monthly climate fields
item.dc:creator: Yu Huang, Shangshang Yang, Sebastian Bathiany, Michael Aich, Philipp Hess, Niklas Boers
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: machine learning, downscaling, extreme event
arXiv:2610.19885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inferring climate fields at higher spatio-temporal resolutions from coarse representations is essential for accessing socioeconomic and environmental impacts. The downscaling of modelled climate fields faces a trade-off between data storage constraints, simulation efficiency, and resolution requirements. While many methods for spatial downscaling have been proposed, joint spatio-temporal downscaling has received comparable little attention. When deriving, for example, daily fields from climate datasets that are available only as monthly averages at coarser spatial resolution, it is highly challenging to faithfully reproduce extreme event statistics and spatiotemporal consistency. To address this task, we introduce a generative machine learning approach, using a diffusion model to jointly downscale monthly temperature and precipitation fields into temporally consistent daily fields at higher spatial resolution. We demonstrate that our approach can generate high-dimensional multivariate climate fields at daily temporal and 0.25{\deg} spatial resolution from monthly input fields at 1{\deg} spatial resolution, exhibiting coherent temporal dynamics and physically plausible spatial structures. In particular, by incorporating a conditional guidance technique, we show that a pre-trained diffusion model can be directly leveraged to efficiently generate daily high-resolution fields conditioned on monthly inputs, without requiring additional fine-tuning or retraining. Our probabilistic approach thus provides an efficient and generalizable framework for spatio-temporal climate downscaling, enabling flexible climate fields generation for climate impact assessments and digital Earth simulator constructions.

item.title: Long-Range Distillation: Distilling 10,000 Years of Simulated Climate into Long Timestep AI Weather Models
item.dc:creator: Scott A. Martin, Noah Brenowitz, Dale Durran, Michael Pritchard
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: predictability, Earth system model, Earth system, reanalysis, ensemble
arXiv:2512.22814v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Accurate long-range weather forecasting remains a major challenge for AI models, both because errors accumulate over autoregressive rollouts and because reanalysis training datasets provide limited sampling of the slow modes of variability underpinning predictability. Most AI and all numerical weather prediction models are autoregressive, repeatedly applying short-lead forecasts to reach subseasonal-to-seasonal (S2S) or seasonal lead times, often causing instability and miscalibration. Long-timestep probabilistic models that generate long-range forecasts in a single step offer an alternative, but training on the 40-year reanalysis record leads to overfitting, suggesting orders of magnitude more data are required. We introduce long-range distillation, whereby a long-timestep probabilistic ``student'' model is trained to forecast directly at long-range using a huge synthetic dataset generated by an autoregressive ``teacher'' model. Using the Deep Learning Earth System Model (DLESyM) as teacher, we generate over 10,000 years of simulated climate to train student models across a range of timescales. In perfect-model experiments, the distilled models outperform climatology and approach their teacher's skill while replacing hundreds of autoregressive steps with a single timestep. In the real world, both a diffusion model student fine-tuned on ERA5 and a linear inverse model student with mixed DLESyM-ERA5 training achieve S2S forecast skill competitive with the ECMWF IFS ensemble, with synthetic pre-training providing improvements beyond ERA5-only training. This demonstrates the benefit of synthetic pre-training for both deep learning and classical data-driven methods, and represents the first demonstration that real-world skill can be improved by training on AI-generated synthetic data in volumes far exceeding the observational record.

item.title: Propagating meteorological uncertainty in physically based mountain snow modeling
item.dc:creator: David R. Casson, Guoqiang Tang, Nicolás Vásquez, Andrew W. Wood, Martyn P. Clark
item.description:
The Cryosphere — matched: data assimilation, emulator, ensemble
Improving mountain snow prediction requires better representation of meteorological uncertainty. This study generates meteorological ensembles accounting for topography, gauge undercatch, and large-scale atmospheric patterns. Driving a physics-based snow model calibrated using a Large Sample Emulator with these ensembles propagates forcing uncertainty into snow accumulation and melt, producing probablistic estimates for data assimilation and hydrological forecasting.

item.title: Njord: A Probabilistic Graph Neural Network for Ensemble Ocean Forecasting
item.dc:creator: Daniel Holmberg, Joel Oskarsson, Erik Wikingsson, Fredrik Lindsten, Teemu Roos
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ensemble, machine learning, neural network
arXiv:2605.15470v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ocean dynamics are inherently chaotic, yet existing machine learning ocean models produce only deterministic forecasts. We introduce Njord, a probabilistic data-driven model for ocean forecasting, applicable to both global and regional domains. Njord combines a deep latent variable framework with a graph neural network architecture, enabling sampling each forecast step in a single forward pass. We apply Njord globally at 0.25{\deg} resolution and regionally to the Baltic Sea at 2 km resolution. To scale to these large ocean grids we introduce K-means cluster meshes that adapt to irregular sea surface geometry. Experiments demonstrate strong performance on both domains compared to deterministic machine learning baselines, while also providing uncertainty estimates from the sampled ensemble forecasts. On the global OceanBench benchmark, Njord achieves the lowest errors on average across upper-ocean variables when evaluated against real-world observations, with the largest improvements in surface temperature prediction.

item.title: A Comprehensive Review on Ice Stupa Technology: Artificial Glacier Systems for Climate-Change Adaptation, Water Security and Sustainable Mountain Development in Cold-Arid Regions
item.dc:creator: Sonam Yangzin, Stanzin Khenrab, Sonam Landol
item.category: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
item.description:
Journal of Scientific Research and Reports — matched: glacier, meltwater, climate change
Cold-arid mountain communities depend heavily on seasonal snow and glacier melt, yet climate-driven changes in cryospheric processes are altering the timing and reliability of water availability. This review critically examines ice stupa technology as an artificial glacier system designed to store winter streamflow as ice and release meltwater during the critical spring irrigation period. The review synthesises evidence on the historical development, physical principles, engineering design, hydrological performance, agricultural relevance, ecological implications, socio-economic dimensions, economics, policy relevance and future research needs of ice stupas. The available evidence indicates that ice-stupa performance is governed primarily by meteorological conditions, surface-energy exchange, hydraulic head and cone geometry. Their compact vertical form can delay ablation, while gravity-fed systems enable operation without pumping energy. Recent advances in automated fountain scheduling substantially improve water-use efficiency and reduce operational failures associated with pipe freezing. However, storage remains primarily village-scale, hydrological performance varies considerably between years and economic, ecological and long-term socio-economic outcomes remain insufficiently quantified. Ice stupas therefore function most appropriately as supplementary seasonal water-storage systems rather than substitutes for natural glaciers or large-scale reservoirs. Their effectiveness depends on careful siting, appropriate engineering, reliable monitoring, community participation and integration with broader catchment-management strategies. Future research should prioritise long-term hydrological monitoring, standardised performance assessment, economic evaluation, ecological measurement and climate-sensitive scaling frameworks.

item.title: Physical Processes Driving Year-to-Year Surface Temperature Variability Changes in a Warming Climate
item.dc:creator: Rory Basinski-Ferris, Ian Eisenman
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: polar, energy balance model, sea ice, ensemble
arXiv:2610.19389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Under anthropogenic greenhouse forcing, climate models project a decrease in year-to-year temperature variability in the mid-to-high latitudes and an increase in the tropics and subtropics. Here, we examine year-to-year temperature variability in the CESM Large Ensemble in concert with an idealized stochastic moist energy balance model (SMEBM) with effective surface heat capacity and local feedback parameter specified based on CESM. We find that the zonal-mean CESM variability change pattern largely persists after filtering out the impact of El Ni\~no. The SMEBM largely captures this change pattern. In the SMEBM, changes in the mid-to-high latitudes are driven by changes in the effective heat capacity due to sea ice retreat, combined with changes in anomalous moist static energy convergence modulated by the polar-amplified time-mean temperature change. The CESM local feedback parameter evolves to be less stabilizing in the low latitudes, which causes tropical and subtropical variability to increase in the SMEBM.

item.title: Collaborative Neural Networks significantly Improve Global Aerosol Retrievals From Multi-Angle Polarimeters
item.dc:creator: Guangliang Fu, Sha Lu, Meng Gao, Jeroen Rietjens, Otto Hasekamp
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: albedo, neural network
arXiv:2610.19217v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the RemoTAP-Hybrid algorithm for global aerosol products retrieved from Multi-Angle Polarimeters (MAP), and apply it to one-year aerosol retrievals from the SPEXone MAP instrument. For the first time, Multiple Collaborated Neural Networks (MCNN) are used to perform global aerosol MAP retrievals over land and ocean. The combined use of MCNN with a full physics inversion in RemoTAP-Hybrid, significantly improves accuracy and computational speed of SPEXone aerosol retrievals. We validate the retrieved Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), Angstrom Exponent (AE), Single Scattering Albedo (SSA), Absorption AOD (AAOD), Fine mode AOD (FAOD), Coarse mode AOD (CAOD), and fine mode effective radius (reff_fine) with AERONET data. The validation suggests that aerosol retrievals can be further improved when extending the aerosol description to include a fine non-spherical mode. For AOD, the Root-Mean-Square Error (RMSE) is 0.051 (0.037) over land (ocean), while 78.3% (80.8%) of the retrievals are within the requirement formulated by the Global Climate Observing System (GCOS). The RMSE is 0.186 (0.207) for AE, 0.038 (0.044) for SSA, 0.023 (0.014) for AAOD, 0.047 (0.031) for FAOD, 0.043 (0.027) for CAOD, and 0.021 (0.026) for reff_fine over land (ocean). Compared to the current RemoTAP algorithm, RemoTAP-Hybrid shows improved agreement with AERONET for AOD, AE, and FAOD over land and ocean while the number of valid retrievals is increased by 4% (3%) over land (ocean) and the computational time is reduced by 43% (32%). Finally, we present the first global seasonal maps of aerosol optical and microphysical properties and chemical composition from SPEXone.

item.title: A performance-based multivariable weighting framework for WRF parameterization-scheme selection
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Gou, Yaoyang Deng, Jun Niu, Shaozhong Kang
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: parameterization
This study proposes a performance-based method to improve WRF climate simulation evaluation by addressing uncertainty in selecting scheme combinations. The method gives greater importance to difficult-to-simulate variables, such as precipitation and wind speed. Tested in two contrasting climate regions, it identified interpretable and well-performing model settings compared with equal weighting and established statistical weighting methods, including in the independent extreme-year test.

item.title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
item.dc:creator: Yuiko Ichikawa, Edward Groot, Jack Atkinson
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: machine learning, neural network
arXiv:2610.19772v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved understanding of compensating errors and the development of more physically consistent weather and climate models.

item.title: High-level, efficient ocean modeling at all scales with Oceananigans
item.dc:creator: Gregory L. Wagner, Simone Silvestri, Navid C. Constantinou, Ali Ramadhan, Jean-Michel Campin, Chris Hill, … (+9)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: ocean circulation, Earth system, numerical method
arXiv:2502.14148v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We describe the user interface, governing equations, and numerical methods underpinning the ocean modeling software called "Oceananigans". Oceananigans development has been led by the Climate Modeling Alliance as part of a larger effort to build a trainable climate model with quantifiable uncertainty. Notably, Oceananigans is written in the Julia programming language, is optimized for GPUs, and can efficiently simulate all scales of ocean motion ranging from millimeter-scale turbulence in a small box to planetary-scale ocean circulation. We argue that this combination of capabilities is enabled by a design that combines a basic, easy-to-optimize, GPU-friendly structured finite volume algorithm exposed behind a high-level, programmable user interface. This design negotiates a dual mandate for highest-possible performance (to support state-of-the-art applications) and enhanced accessibility (to facilitate adoption and development). The dual mandate aims ultimately to accelerate the progress of Earth system science.

item.title: Cosmic Rays as an Interdisciplinary Earth Observation Tool: From Particle Physics and Atmospheric Processes to Geosciences and Urban Science
item.dc:creator: Bugra Bilin, Nuhcan Ak\c{c}it
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: cosmogenic, remote sensing
arXiv:2601.19265v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The exploration of cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles originating from space and the atmosphere, has historically been associated with particle physics and astrophysics. In the last 20 years, these particles have evolved into valuable tools for observing Earth's systems. This review compiles the use of cosmic rays in three primary areas: (1) particle physics and atmospheric processes, which include cosmic- ray-induced cascades, ionization, and their impact on atmospheric chemistry and radiation; (2) geosciences, where cosmogenic radionuclides assist in the dating of geological materials and cosmic-ray neutrons are used for large-scale monitoring of soil moisture and snow water equivalents; and (3) urban science, where cosmic- ray muons are employed for non-invasive subsurface imaging and, when paired with distributed sensors, serve as the basis for smart city monitoring. This review places particular emphasis on integrating these methods with remote sensing and geographic information systems (GIS), which helps close the persistent scale gap between point measurements and satellite observations, thereby enabling three-dimensional digital representations of subsurfaces. This review concludes by discussing data standards, their integration into operational Earth observation workflows, and future research directions.

item.title: PrecipCorrDiff: A Deep Learning Framework for Generating 0.0625$^\circ$ High-Resolution IMD Gridded Precipitation Data
item.dc:creator: Bipin Kumar, Rajib Chattopadhyay, Harsh P. Bachhav, Jannu, Bhupendra Bahadur Singh, Ramesh Ragala, … (+4)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: downscaling
arXiv:2610.19994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-resolution precipitation datasets are essential for weather forecasting, hydrological modeling, and climate risk assessment, yet observation-based gridded products often lack the spatial detail required for regional applications. Here we present PrecipCorrDiff, a diffusion-based downscaling framework built by modifying the original corrector diffusion based archetecture that incorporates a customized loss function and a multi-scale residual generation strategy to improve the precipitation especially the representation of extremes. PrecipCorrDiff generates 0.0625{\deg} resolution India Meteorological Department (IMD) precipitation fields from 0.25{\deg} gridded data while preserving precipitation statistics and reconstructing fine-scale spatial variability. Validation against independent IMD station observations, comparing the proposed framework with the SRGAN-based model and the original CorrDiff model, indicates that the proposed framework substantially improves the representation of spatial precipitation patterns, rainfall intensity distributions, and extreme rainfall events, while eliminating the systematic negative bias present in the previously developed SRGAN-based model. Across four climatologically distinct homogeneous Indian monsoon regions, PrecipCorrDiff reproduces observed precipitation characteristics with near-zero spatial bias, demonstrating the potential of diffusion-based downscaling for generating physically consistent, high-resolution precipitation datasets for hydrological, meteorological, and climate applications.

item.title: Improved Precipitation Variability in the Community Atmosphere Model through Implementation of a Neural-Network Deep Convection Scheme
item.dc:creator: Xavier J. Levine, Griffin Mooers, Jack W. Atkinson, Marat F. Khairoutdinov, Janni Yuval, Dominic Orchard, … (+1)
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: parameterization, neural network
arXiv:2610.20405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conventional deep convection schemes remain a primary source of uncertainty in global climate models, yet replacing them with data-driven alternatives while maintaining physical consistency and numerical stability is an open challenge. We present a hybrid configuration of the Community Atmosphere Model version 6 (CAM6), in which a fully connected deep neural network replaces the Zhang-McFarlane deep convection scheme (ZM), while radiation, turbulence, and other cloud processes are left unchanged. The network is trained on output from a storm-resolving global model - the global System for Atmospheric Modeling (gSAM) - using a coarse-graining approach to derive subgrid-scale convective fluxes and tendencies. This data-driven parameterization is ported to CAM6 and found to run stably for more than a decade while conserving energy and moisture. It produces a broadly realistic climatology without retuning the remaining parameterizations. Relative to the default Zhang-McFarlane scheme, the neural network parameterization substantially improves some long-standing model deficiencies. In particular, the biases in light precipitation and extreme precipitation are markedly reduced, and the diurnal cycle of tropical land precipitation shifts from a spurious midday peak over many regions to the observed late-afternoon peak. These results support targeted ML-based convection schemes as a viable path toward reducing systematic model errors in next-generation climate models.

item.title: Quantitative Reconstruction of Late Miocene Monsoon‐Driven Climate and Hydrology in the Himalayan Foreland, Nepal
item.dc:creator: Purushottam Adhikari, Gaurav Srivastava, Sujata Poudel, Harshita Bhatia, Roshan Paudel, Basant Kunwar, … (+3)
item.description:
Paleoceanography and Paleoclimatology — matched: paleoclimate
Abstract The Late Miocene was a critical interval in the evolution of the South Asian monsoon system and the Himalayan foreland. This study presents a quantitative paleoclimatic reconstruction based on fossil leaf assemblages from the Lower (10.5–9.2 Ma) and Middle (9.2–7.0 Ma) Siwalik sediments of the Daldale section, western Nepal, using the Climate Leaf Analysis Multivariate Program (CLAMP). The reconstructed mean annual temperatures are 22.2 ± 2.3°C for the Lower Siwalik and 21.5 ± 2.3°C for the Middle Siwalik, with corresponding cold month mean temperatures of 15.4 ± 3.3°C and 15.0 ± 3.3°C. Mean annual precipitation ranges from 228 ± 48 to 238 ± 48 cm, and the annual vapor pressure deficit remains close to 6 ± 2 hPa, indicating persistently warm and humid monsoon‐influenced conditions throughout the study interval. Although several climatic variables exhibit coherent directional trends, including slightly lower temperatures, reduced rainfall concentration during the wettest months, and subtle changes in seasonal moisture availability in the Middle Siwalik, these differences largely overlap within the uncertainties of the CLAMP reconstructions. Consequently, the Daldale record indicates broad climatic stability rather than a major climatic transition between the Lower and Middle Siwalik intervals within the studied section. The study provides the first quantitative paleoclimatic benchmark for the Daldale Siwalik succession and demonstrates that climatic responses within the Himalayan foreland were spatially heterogeneous, with western Nepal maintaining persistently humid conditions despite broader regional environmental changes.

item.title: Improving snow simulations through improved representations of vegetation conditions: insights from high resolution simulations over California
item.dc:creator: Aniket Gupta, Ali Behrangi, Mohammad Farmani, Patrick Broxton, Guo-Yue Niu
item.description:
The Cryosphere
Most hydrological models tend to underestimate snow over the mountainous southwestern US. This may result from uncertainties in precipitation forcing and/or inadequate representation of snow–vegetation interactions, particularly canopy interception and shading. Through model experiments, we demonstrate how downscaled meteorological forcing and improved vegetation representation can improve snow simulations over the southwestern US.

item.title: TRAILS – a novel framework for time-height-resolved attribution of long-range transported wildfire smoke
item.dc:creator: Johanna Roschke, Benedikt Gast, Martin Radenz, Albert Ansmann, Patric Seifert, George McCosh, … (+1)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
This research introduces a new method that combines model simulations with satellite observations to attribute the influence of wildfire smoke on an airmass. By dynamically determining the height of smoke plumes, we overcome a key limitation of earlier fixed reception-height approaches. This advancement is crucial for improving our understanding of how wildfire emissions influence cloud formation and the broader Earth's climate system.
